entries.verseWEB: Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.
entries.verseKJV: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
entries.pullMedium: Don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself.
entries.pullLong: Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.
entries.explanation: Jesus says this to people who genuinely did not know where the next meal was coming from, so it is not advice for the mildly stressed. What he points out is practical: worry borrows a burden from a day that has not arrived, and it never makes that day easier when it does. The instruction he leaves you is small. Handle today. Tomorrow gets its own attention when it becomes today.
entries.question: Where are you already carrying tomorrow?

entries.verseWEB: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
entries.verseKJV: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
entries.pullMedium: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer...
entries.pullLong: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
entries.explanation: Paul writes to people who faced real hardships, encouraging them to replace anxiety with prayer. This isn't about avoiding struggles but about transforming how you handle them. When you take your worries and turn them into conversations with God, you create space for peace. Imagine sitting with a friend and sharing your troubles over coffee. This act of connection can shift your focus from stress to gratitude, bringing calm that doesn't rely on circumstances.
entries.question: What worry would you say out loud first?

entries.verseWEB: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.
entries.verseKJV: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
entries.pullMedium: He makes me lie down in green pastures.
entries.pullLong: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
entries.explanation: Ancient shepherds were responsible for the safety and well-being of their sheep, guiding them to nourishment and rest. This imagery gives comfort when anxiety looms. You can imagine yourself being gently led to a peaceful spot, a moment when your mind is at ease. It's about recognizing those moments of calm in your day, like when you take a walk or enjoy a hot tea. These are reminders that you are cared for.
entries.question: Where do you find moments of calm today?

entries.verseWEB: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.
entries.verseKJV: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
entries.pullMedium: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.
entries.pullLong: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.
entries.explanation: Peter wrote this to people facing real danger, reminding them they are not alone. When anxiety feels overwhelming, this verse says someone cares deeply about you, and wants the weight handed over. Like telling a friend what is really going on, saying it to God shares the load. Maybe tonight, lying awake listing everything that could go wrong, you name each worry instead of holding it. It is not ignoring problems. It is refusing to face them by yourself.
entries.question: Who helps you carry your worries?

entries.verseWEB: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
entries.verseKJV: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
entries.pullShort: Don’t be afraid, for I am with you.
entries.pullMedium: Don’t be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed.
entries.pullLong: Don’t be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you.
entries.explanation: Israel heard these words in exile, far from home and afraid of what came next. The promise is not an easy path. It is company on a hard one: strength for the part of the road you are actually standing on. Maybe the week ahead holds a conversation you dread or a bill you cannot yet cover. The verse does not shrink those. It says you will not be walking into them alone.
entries.question: When have you felt strengthened unexpectedly?

entries.verseWEB: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
entries.verseKJV: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
entries.pullMedium: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened.
entries.pullLong: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
entries.explanation: In a time when physical labor was exhausting and life was demanding, this passage offers an alternative to relentless striving. It's about finding relief from burdens by taking on something that is surprisingly light. Imagine a week already too full by breakfast on its second day. This passage suggests that some burdens aren't meant to be carried alone. The relief isn't necessarily in doing less, but in how you approach what you have to do.
entries.question: Which burdens feel heavy for you today?

entries.verseWEB: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
entries.verseKJV: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
entries.pullShort: near to those who have a broken heart
entries.pullMedium: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart
entries.pullLong: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
entries.explanation: This verse acknowledges the deep pain of those feeling broken and overwhelmed. It speaks to the comfort available when life feels heavy, like when you're sitting in your car after a hard day, feeling like you can't face anything else. The verse assures that in moments of deep sorrow, there is closeness and understanding. The comfort is in knowing you're not alone, even in the depths of anxiety and heartache.
entries.question: How do you find comfort when you're overwhelmed?

entries.verseWEB: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
entries.verseKJV: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
entries.pullMedium: Trust in the LORD with all your heart.
entries.pullLong: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
entries.explanation: This passage speaks to the challenge of trusting beyond what you can see or figure out. It’s about acknowledging a source of guidance greater than your own insight. Imagine deciding whether to take a new job. You weigh the pros and cons, but the decision feels heavy. Here, the advice is to trust that more is at work than just your understanding. It’s less about ignoring facts and more about allowing for possibilities beyond them.
entries.question: Where do you struggle to trust beyond sight?

entries.verseWEB: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.
entries.verseKJV: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
entries.pullMedium: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.
entries.pullLong: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you, acknowledging fear and choosing trust.
entries.explanation: Feeling afraid is a natural part of life, just like when your heart races before a big presentation or a difficult conversation. The psalmist acknowledges fear but chooses a practical response: trust. It's about redirecting your focus. Imagine placing your fear in a mental box labeled 'trust' before starting your day. This doesn't eliminate fear but offers a way to face it. Trust becomes a choice you make repeatedly, especially when fear feels overwhelming.
entries.question: How can trust reshape your fear today?

entries.verseWEB: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
entries.verseKJV: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
entries.pullMedium: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace
entries.pullLong: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
entries.explanation: In a time of uncertainty, the promise of peace is powerful. It's about having a stable mindset, not because life is easy, but because trust is placed on something steadfast. Think of a day when everything goes wrong, yet you find calm by relying on what is unshakeable. This isn't about ignoring problems but about finding a center that doesn't shift. Trust brings peace not by changing the situation, but by changing how you meet it.
entries.question: Where do you seek peace in uncertainty?

entries.verseWEB: Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us. Selah.
entries.verseKJV: Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
entries.pullShort: God is a refuge for us.
entries.pullMedium: Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge.
entries.pullLong: Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us.
entries.explanation: In a world filled with uncertainties, this verse encourages you to bring your worries and fears to God. It's about finding a safe space where you can express your thoughts without judgment. Like confiding in a close friend, this pouring out can happen during a quiet moment on a walk or while sipping a morning coffee. You're reminded that you're not alone in your struggles, and there is comfort in knowing you can share them.
entries.question: What would you pour out today?

entries.verseWEB: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, and whose confidence is in the LORD. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.
entries.verseKJV: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
entries.pullMedium: Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD
entries.pullLong: Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, and whose confidence is in the LORD.
entries.explanation: Jeremiah paints a picture of stability and resilience. Just like a tree by a river thrives despite harsh conditions, trust in God provides stability when life gets tough. You may find yourself in a challenging meeting at work, uncertain of the outcome. Trust isn't about ignoring reality but finding a steady source of strength that keeps you grounded, ensuring you can still produce good, even in dry times.
entries.question: Where do you find your stability daily?

entries.verseWEB: Those who know your name will put their trust in you, for you, LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you.
entries.verseKJV: And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, LORD, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.
entries.pullMedium: Those who know your name will put their trust in you
entries.pullLong: Those who know your name will put their trust in you, for you, LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you.
entries.explanation: The Psalmist talks about trust built on experience. Those who have seen reliability in past trials find it easier to trust for the future. Imagine a friend who always shows up when needed. Over time, you naturally trust them more. This verse reflects that kind of trust. Somewhere in an ordinary day, recall a time you were carried when you asked. It's a reminder that reliability builds trust, and seeking help has been met with support.
entries.question: When have you been supported in the past?

entries.verseWEB: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.
entries.verseKJV: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
entries.pullMedium: The LORD is a stronghold in the day of trouble
entries.pullLong: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.
entries.explanation: Nahum speaks to people facing real threats and uncertainty. He describes a trustworthy refuge in times of trouble, comparing it to a stronghold. Imagine a stretch when the deadlines stack faster than you can clear them. Finding a quiet moment or a supportive friend can be your stronghold, a place where you feel understood and safe. The core idea is about finding security and peace in places or people that truly know you.
entries.question: Where do you find refuge when stressed?

entries.verseWEB: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted amongst the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.”
entries.verseKJV: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
entries.pullMedium: Be still, and know that I am God.
entries.pullLong: Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted amongst the nations.
entries.explanation: This psalm speaks to people facing chaos and uncertainty, urging them to pause and recognize a greater presence. It's not about inactivity but about finding calm amid life's storms. In the middle of a loud day, a single quiet minute, phone face down, can hand back perspective. This stillness can remind you of the bigger picture and the stability it offers, despite daily pressures.
entries.question: How can you find stillness today?

entries.verseWEB: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me live in safety.
entries.verseKJV: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
entries.pullShort: In peace I will lay down
entries.pullMedium: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep
entries.pullLong: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me live in safety.
entries.explanation: In a world that feels chaotic, finding rest can be challenging. This verse reflects a moment of deep trust, where the writer chooses peace over anxiety. Picture lying in bed, your mind racing with unfinished tasks, yet deliberately choosing to release those worries. The belief here is that safety isn't based on circumstances, but on a deeper assurance. It's about allowing yourself to truly rest, knowing that you are held securely.
entries.question: What keeps you awake at night?

entries.verseWEB: The fear of the LORD leads to life, then contentment; he rests and will not be touched by trouble.
entries.verseKJV: The fear of the LORD tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil.
entries.pullMedium: The fear of the LORD leads to life, then contentment
entries.pullLong: The fear of the LORD leads to life, then contentment; he rests and will not be touched by trouble.
entries.explanation: This proverb speaks to a life anchored in reverence, leading to a deep sense of contentment. It’s not about avoiding trouble but finding a type of peace that keeps you steady. Imagine finishing your workday, feeling satisfied with what you’ve done. You’re not chasing more because you’ve embraced enough. This contentment brings a restful state, where worries don’t easily shake you. It’s about finding calm in the midst of life's chaos.
entries.question: Where do you find contentment today?

entries.verseWEB: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
entries.verseKJV: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
entries.pullMedium: Come to me... and I will give you rest.
entries.pullLong: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
entries.explanation: This verse offers a promise of rest to those feeling overwhelmed by life's demands. Picture a busy day where everything feels too much. Instead of pushing harder, you pause and share your burdens with someone who understands. It's not about escaping responsibilities but finding relief in knowing you're not alone. This rest is about sharing the load, not removing it completely. Sometimes, just taking a moment to breathe can make all the difference.
entries.question: What burden could you share today?

entries.verseWEB: He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
entries.verseKJV: And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
entries.pullMedium: Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.
entries.pullLong: He said to them, "Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile." For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
entries.explanation: The disciples were busy, surrounded by crowds and constant demands. Jesus noticed they were so occupied, they didn't have time to eat. He invited them to take a break in a quiet place. This wasn't about escaping responsibilities but recognizing the need for physical and mental rest. Imagine stepping outside mid afternoon for ten unhurried minutes of walking. That break refreshes you, even if briefly, allowing you to return with renewed focus.
entries.question: Where can you find a quiet moment today?

entries.verseWEB: There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.
entries.verseKJV: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.
entries.pullShort: A Sabbath rest for the people
entries.pullMedium: There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
entries.pullLong: There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.
entries.explanation: The writer of Hebrews talks about a rest that goes beyond just taking a day off. This rest is similar to how God rested after creation. It means stopping continual efforts to earn peace or approval, knowing that it's already been given. Imagine choosing one evening this week to let the list go unfinished. You recognize that sometimes, stepping back is the most productive step forward, allowing you to recharge and gain clarity.
entries.question: How can you pause and truly rest today?

entries.verseWEB: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honourable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.
entries.verseKJV: Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
entries.pullMedium: whatever things are true, whatever things are honourable
entries.pullLong: whatever things are true, whatever things are honourable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely
entries.explanation: Paul encourages focusing on positive and uplifting thoughts. This is practical for days when negativity seems overwhelming, like the low hour of a working afternoon. Instead of dwelling on frustrations, intentionally find something good—a kind word from a friend or a moment of laughter. This shift won't change the situation, but it can change your perspective, offering a sense of rest from mental clutter.
entries.question: What positive thought can you focus on today?

entries.verseWEB: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
entries.verseKJV: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
entries.pullShort: God is our refuge and strength
entries.pullMedium: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help
entries.pullLong: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
entries.explanation: This passage speaks to moments when you feel exhausted and overwhelmed. It paints a picture of God as a refuge—a place to find safety and renewal. Think about how you might take a few minutes during a hectic day to pause and seek peace, much like stepping into a shelter from a storm. This presence isn't distant; it's close, accessible when trouble arises, offering strength you can't find alone.
entries.question: Where do you find refuge when overwhelmed?

entries.verseWEB: I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
entries.verseKJV: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
entries.pullShort: lift up my eyes to the hills
entries.pullMedium: I will lift up my eyes to the hills.
entries.pullLong: I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?
entries.explanation: This psalm reflects a moment of seeking strength beyond oneself. When you're feeling drained, looking up—literally or metaphorically—can remind you of sources of support that are bigger than the immediate problem. The writer finds reassurance in recognizing that help comes from a powerful creator. On a hard day, acknowledging where your help comes from might be one slow breath and a lifted gaze.
entries.question: Where do you look when you're feeling depleted?

entries.verseWEB: The LORD’s name is a strong tower: the righteous run to him, and are safe.
entries.verseKJV: The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
entries.pullMedium: The LORD’s name is a strong tower.
entries.pullLong: The LORD’s name is a strong tower: the righteous run to him, and are safe.
entries.explanation: Imagine being completely worn out from a long day, and then you find a safe place to rest. This verse describes how the name of the Lord serves as that sanctuary. It’s like having a reliable refuge that offers protection and peace when you feel overwhelmed. This is not just for crises but also for the everyday moments when you feel drained. Finding a moment of peace allows you to recharge and continue.
entries.question: Where do you find refuge when exhausted?

entries.verseWEB: Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
entries.verseKJV: But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.
entries.pullShort: With God all things are possible.
entries.pullMedium: With God all things are possible.
entries.pullLong: With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
entries.explanation: In this passage, Jesus talks to people facing a task they considered impossible. He's not promising easy success but highlighting that human limits aren't the final word. Imagine you're stuck on a work project that seems to have no solution. This verse invites you to consider possibilities beyond your own ability. When you feel depleted, remember that the outcomes aren't solely on your shoulders. There's room to believe in possibilities outside your control.
entries.question: Where do you see limits blocking possibilities?

entries.verseWEB: I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”
entries.verseKJV: These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
entries.pullMedium: In the world you have trouble; but cheer up!
entries.pullLong: I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up!
entries.explanation: Jesus acknowledges that life is full of challenges, which isn't always comforting when you're drained and weary. The reminder is that peace is found in him, not in the absence of trouble. Think of a day when everything goes wrong, like your car breaking down or a deadline looming. Knowing that there's a bigger picture can help you handle those moments with a bit more calm. It's not about avoiding trouble but finding peace amid it.
entries.question: Where do you look for peace?

entries.verseWEB: He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me. Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.
entries.verseKJV: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.
entries.pullShort: My grace is sufficient for you
entries.pullMedium: My power is made perfect in weakness.
entries.pullLong: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.
entries.explanation: Paul had something painful he begged God three times to remove. The answer was not removal. It was grace enough to live with it, and a strength that shows up precisely where his ran out. So he stopped hiding the weak places. Maybe there is a limitation you spend real energy concealing, a struggle, a need for help. This passage is not celebrating hardship. It is saying the concealed place is where the carrying strength arrives.
entries.question: When have you found strength in weakness?

entries.verseWEB: that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
entries.verseKJV: That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man;
entries.pullMedium: strengthened with power through his Spirit
entries.pullLong: that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person
entries.explanation: Paul is praying for people he loves, and what he asks for is not ease. He asks that they be strengthened on the inside, in the place circumstances cannot reach. Outward things run down: energy, patience, the week itself. The prayer assumes an inner room that can be resupplied while all of that is still true. Maybe you are running on reserves lately. This passage says the deepest part of you is exactly where renewal is offered.
entries.question: Where do you seek your inner strength?

entries.verseWEB: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
entries.verseKJV: NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
entries.pullMedium: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light.
entries.pullLong: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
entries.explanation: In a world full of choices, finding direction can be daunting. This verse speaks to the practical help found in scripture. Like a flashlight on a dim path, it offers clarity for your next step, not the entire journey. Imagine deciding on a new job opportunity. While you may not see the whole future, guidance from scripture can illuminate what aligns with your values today. Trust that clarity for the next step will come.
entries.question: How is scripture lighting your choices today?

entries.verseWEB: A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps.
entries.verseKJV: A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
entries.pullMedium: A man’s heart plans his course
entries.pullLong: A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps.
entries.explanation: In life, you often make plans about what you want to achieve, much like deciding to start a new project at work. However, things don't always go as expected. This verse suggests that while you decide on your path, the actual steps you take may be influenced by unforeseen circumstances or opportunities. This doesn't undermine your plans but adds an element of flexibility and trust in the journey that unfolds.
entries.question: How do you respond when plans change?

entries.verseWEB: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you. For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
entries.verseKJV: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
entries.pullShort: Ask, and it will be given you.
entries.pullMedium: Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened.
entries.pullLong: Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
entries.explanation: In this passage, Jesus encourages people to actively seek help and guidance rather than passively waiting for solutions. Imagine you're facing a tough decision at work. Instead of worrying, you might ask a colleague for advice, research options, or even pray for clarity. The process of asking, seeking, and knocking is about being proactive in finding answers and opportunities. This passage reassures that effort is not in vain and help is available.
entries.question: Where can you actively seek guidance today?

entries.verseWEB: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
entries.verseKJV: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
entries.pullMedium: I am the way, the truth, and the life...
entries.pullLong: I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
entries.explanation: When you face big decisions, guidance can feel elusive. Here, Jesus talks about a singular path, emphasizing clarity in direction. It's like choosing between a well-marked highway and a confusing maze. In everyday terms, this means considering what aligns with core truths when you're unsure. It can be as small as pausing before answering a difficult message, choosing the honest reply over the clever one. This passage reassures that clarity exists amidst uncertainty.
entries.question: What decision needs clarity today?

entries.verseWEB: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
entries.verseKJV: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
entries.pullMedium: ask of God, who gives to all liberally
entries.pullLong: ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
entries.explanation: You face decisions that leave you unsure of what to do. James offers a simple approach: ask for wisdom. Wisdom is not just knowledge, but the ability to decide and act well. It's reassuring to know that this wisdom is offered generously, without criticism, when you ask. Imagine needing guidance about a work decision or a family issue. The comfort lies in knowing you can ask for clarity and trust it will come.
entries.question: Where do you need wisdom right now?

entries.pullLong: I hope in his word. My soul longs for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning.
entries.explanation: In ancient times, watchmen stood guard through the night, eagerly anticipating the morning light. This passage captures that deep longing and anticipation. On a regular Tuesday, you might find yourself waiting for important news or a change in a difficult situation. The psalmist describes a soul that waits with hope, anchored in the assurance found in God's word. This isn't passive waiting but an active hope, much like watchmen knowing dawn will surely come.
entries.question: What are you waiting for with deep anticipation?

entries.verseWEB: In his name, the nations will hope.”
entries.verseKJV: And in his name shall the Gentiles trust.
entries.pullMedium: In his name, the nations will hope.
entries.pullLong: In his name, the nations will hope.
entries.explanation: Matthew talks about a future where hope is not confined to one group but spreads across nations. It suggests a kind of hope that transcends borders and differences, offering a sense of unity and peace. Think about a time when you felt everyone was pulling together, perhaps during a community event. That shared hope can be a powerful force, reminding you that you're part of something bigger, woven into a global tapestry of hope.
entries.question: Where do you find shared hope today?

entries.verseWEB: For nothing spoken by God is impossible.”
entries.verseKJV: For with God nothing shall be impossible.
entries.pullMedium: For nothing spoken by God is impossible.
entries.pullLong: For nothing spoken by God is impossible.
entries.explanation: Gabriel tells Mary that nothing spoken by God is impossible, as she grapples with the news of her miraculous pregnancy. This is not about small everyday hopes, but about profound, life-altering promises. On an ordinary Tuesday, you might face situations that seem beyond reach. This verse reminds you that outcomes can surprise you in unexpected ways. Believing in possibilities can keep you open to what unfolds, even when it seems improbable.
entries.question: What seems impossible in your life right now?

entries.verseWEB: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.
entries.verseKJV: Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.
entries.pullShort: fill you with all joy and peace
entries.pullMedium: fill you with all joy and peace in believing
entries.pullLong: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope.
entries.explanation: Paul writes to people whose lives were not easy, encouraging them to find joy and peace through belief. In everyday terms, it's like finding quiet in a busy day by focusing on what you know to be true. On a regular Tuesday, maybe you pause to appreciate small wins, like finishing a task or enjoying a good conversation. This creates a hopeful outlook, seeing that good things are possible, even when life feels overwhelming.
entries.question: Where do you find small moments of hope daily?

entries.verseWEB: Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish you in every good work and word.
entries.verseKJV: Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, which hath loved us, and hath given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace, Comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work.
entries.pullMedium: eternal comfort and good hope through grace
entries.pullLong: our Lord Jesus Christ... gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts
entries.explanation: Paul encourages a community facing uncertainty by highlighting the eternal comfort and hope that God offers through grace. This isn't about escaping challenges but finding reassurance and strength amidst them. On a Tuesday, you might face a demanding project or difficult news, yet this passage reminds you that comfort and hope are constants, grounding you in your actions and words. It's about being steady, knowing you're supported.
entries.question: Where do you find comfort amid challenges?

entries.verseWEB: let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful.
entries.verseKJV: Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
entries.pullShort: hold fast the confession of our hope
entries.pullMedium: hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering
entries.pullLong: let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful.
entries.explanation: The writer of Hebrews encourages people who face uncertainty to cling to hope. In daily life, this might mean keeping faith in promises when situations seem shaky. Like trusting a friend to show up as planned, even if the weather looks bad. You hold onto hope because past experiences show reliability. It’s not blind optimism. It’s based on what you’ve seen before. Hope grows stronger when anchored in past faithfulness.
entries.question: What reinforces your hope today?

entries.verseWEB: The LORD is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
entries.verseKJV: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
entries.pullMedium: The LORD is my light and my salvation.
entries.pullLong: The LORD is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life.
entries.explanation: The writer of this psalm finds reassurance in the idea that they are not alone in facing life's challenges. Imagine you are about to give a big presentation at work. The nerves might creep in, but knowing that your strength isn't solely your own can be comforting. The verse highlights that there's a source of courage beyond personal capability. The presence of a guiding light makes it easier to step forward, even when uncertain.
entries.question: What's one thing that scares you today?

entries.verseWEB: In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?
entries.verseKJV: In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.
entries.pullMedium: In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid.
entries.pullLong: In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid.
entries.explanation: David faced real threats and danger when he wrote this. His choice to trust instead of fear wasn't made in a safe space, but in a turbulent one. On a Tuesday, when you're worried about a difficult meeting or a health concern, this verse reminds you that trust isn't about ignoring reality but about choosing where to place your focus. Trusting in something bigger than human threats can bring peace.
entries.question: Where might trust replace your fear today?

entries.verseWEB: The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in the LORD is kept safe.
entries.verseKJV: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
entries.pullShort: The fear of man proves a snare,
entries.pullMedium: The fear of man proves to be a snare, but trust in the LORD is safe.
entries.pullLong: The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in the LORD is kept safe.
entries.explanation: Proverbs 29:25 highlights how fear of others' opinions or actions can trap you in a cycle of anxiety and people-pleasing. Imagine a day when you're worried about a coworker's judgment on your project. This fear can limit your creativity and confidence. Trust, however, in something bigger, like a principle or value, provides a steadier ground. It’s about finding safety in integrity rather than in trying to manage others' perceptions.
entries.question: Whose opinion do you fear most today?

entries.verseWEB: “Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father’s will. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore don’t be afraid. You are of more value than many sparrows.
entries.verseKJV: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.
entries.pullMedium: You are of more value than many sparrows.
entries.pullLong: Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father’s will. You are of more value than many sparrows.
entries.explanation: In a time when people often felt insignificant, Jesus used sparrows to illustrate value. Sparrows were cheap, yet not unnoticed. He reminded them that God is aware of even the smallest details, like the number of hairs on your head. This isn't about being fearless, but understanding that your worth is recognized. On a Tuesday, when you feel overlooked, remember you have intrinsic value that doesn't go unnoticed.
entries.question: How do you feel valued today?

entries.verseWEB: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.
entries.verseKJV: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
entries.pullMedium: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you.
entries.pullLong: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you.
entries.explanation: Facing uncertainty, you might wish for a peace that holds steady. In this verse, Jesus offers a peace that’s different from what you find in the world. It’s not about circumstances being perfect; it’s deeper, internal. On an ordinary Tuesday, you might feel anxious about a meeting or a decision. Remember, this peace isn’t tied to the success of the day. It’s a calm that exists alongside whatever happens.
entries.question: What brings you peace amidst fear today?

entries.verseWEB: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
entries.verseKJV: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
entries.pullMedium: Neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities
entries.pullLong: Neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come
entries.explanation: Paul addresses a deep fear: the fear of being separated from love. His words reassure that nothing—no force or circumstance—can come between you and the love found in Christ. On any ordinary day, when you're feeling isolated or overwhelmed, remember that this love is a constant. It doesn't hinge on anything you do or face. You're tethered to something unshakeable, even when fear suggests otherwise.
entries.question: What fear feels like separation today?

entries.verseWEB: For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
entries.verseKJV: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
entries.pullMedium: a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control
entries.pullLong: For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
entries.explanation: Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader facing genuine challenges and pressures. The encouragement is clear: fear should not define or limit you. Instead, there is a power available that brings strength, love, and self-discipline. On an ordinary day, this might mean tackling a difficult task at work with a mindset of capability and calm, rather than being overwhelmed by anxiety. This perspective is about the resources you have, not the obstacles.
entries.question: Where is fear limiting your actions today?

entries.verseWEB: There are many plans in a man’s heart, but the LORD’s counsel will prevail.
entries.verseKJV: There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
entries.pullMedium: There are many plans in a man’s heart, but the LORD’s counsel will prevail.
entries.pullLong: There are many plans in a man’s heart, but the LORD’s counsel will prevail.
entries.explanation: You may find yourself planning your week, juggling appointments, and setting goals. Yet, this proverb reminds you that no matter how detailed the plans, life's unpredictability still holds sway. It's not about abandoning plans but recognizing that unexpected turns are part of the journey. When a meeting gets canceled or a task takes longer than expected, it's an opportunity to remember that not all disruptions are setbacks. Some are just part of a bigger picture that's unfolding.
entries.question: How do you handle unexpected changes today?

entries.verseWEB: The LORD will fulfil that which concerns me. Your loving kindness, LORD, endures forever. Don’t forsake the works of your own hands.
entries.verseKJV: The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands.
entries.pullMedium: The LORD will fulfil that which concerns me.
entries.pullLong: The LORD will fulfil that which concerns me. Your loving kindness, LORD, endures forever.
entries.explanation: This psalm is about trusting that what matters to you matters to a higher power, and that enduring care is at work. Imagine a Tuesday where you're tangled in life's unpredictability. You might wonder if you're hitting the right notes in your purpose and calling. This verse suggests that your efforts are not forgotten. They're part of something bigger, and there's an enduring kindness that won't leave them unfinished.
entries.question: Where do you see unfinished work in your life?

entries.verseWEB: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
entries.verseKJV: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
entries.pullShort: You are the light of the world.
entries.pullMedium: A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
entries.pullLong: Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines.
entries.explanation: Jesus uses everyday objects like lamps and cities to explain your influence. Just like a lamp provides light to a room, your actions can illuminate your community. On a typical Tuesday, consider how a simple act of kindness at work or in your neighborhood might brighten someone's day. The impact of these small gestures can be more significant than you realize, encouraging others to notice something greater behind your actions.
entries.question: How can your actions positively influence others?

entries.verseWEB: You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you.
entries.verseKJV: Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
entries.pullMedium: "I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit"
entries.pullLong: "You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain"
entries.explanation: This is about being chosen for a purpose, not just chosen. Jesus is speaking to those he has given a task—bearing fruit that lasts. It's less about personal achievement and more about purposeful living. Imagine a Tuesday where your work or interactions feel meaningless. This verse suggests a different view: your actions have lasting impact, even in small ways. It's about understanding that your everyday efforts can be part of something bigger.
entries.question: What lasting impact are you making today?

entries.verseWEB: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.
entries.verseKJV: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
entries.pullShort: all things work together for good
entries.pullMedium: all things work together for good for those who love God
entries.pullLong: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.
entries.explanation: Paul writes this to people who faced real hardships and uncertainties. The message is not that everything feels good now, but that there's a larger purpose at play. On a regular Tuesday, when plans fall apart or unexpected challenges arise, you can pause and remember that this moment has meaning beyond itself. It's about finding a sense of peace in knowing there's a bigger picture, even when that's hard to see.
entries.question: Where can you find meaning in today’s events?

entries.verseWEB: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
entries.verseKJV: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
entries.pullShort: created in Christ Jesus for good works
entries.pullMedium: created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared
entries.pullLong: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
entries.explanation: Before you did anything, Paul says, you were already workmanship: made on purpose, with good work prepared ahead of you like a path laid before a walker. That reframes an overwhelming week. The tasks in front of you are not random obligations to survive. Some of them are the very things you were shaped for, waiting where you would find them. You do not have to feel sure of your day for that to be true of it.
entries.question: How do you see purpose in your daily tasks?

entries.verseWEB: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on towards the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
entries.verseKJV: Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
entries.pullShort: forgetting the things which are behind
entries.pullMedium: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward
entries.pullLong: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on
entries.explanation: Paul talks about not dwelling on the past but focusing on what lies ahead. Imagine you've just spilled coffee on your shirt before a big meeting. You could fixate on the stain or focus on the presentation. Paul suggests that life is about moving forward, not being trapped by previous missteps or successes. His goal is about pressing toward a higher calling, not perfection. Today, you can make progress without being perfect.
entries.question: What past event are you still holding onto?

entries.verseWEB: In all hard work there is profit, but the talk of the lips leads only to poverty.
entries.verseKJV: In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
entries.pullShort: In all hard work there is profit
entries.pullMedium: In all hard work there is profit, but the talk of the lips...
entries.pullLong: In all hard work there is profit, but the talk of the lips leads only to poverty.
entries.explanation: This proverb addresses the value of hard work versus mere talk. In your daily life, you might find yourself discussing plans and goals with friends or colleagues, but without action, those words remain just ideas. Imagine spending an afternoon organizing your workspace instead of just talking about it. The effort you put in adds real value, while idle chatter doesn't get you anywhere. It's a reminder that tangible results come from doing, not just discussing.
entries.question: Where are you talking without acting?

entries.verseWEB: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.
entries.verseKJV: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
entries.pullMedium: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might.
entries.pullLong: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work, nor plan, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, where you are going.
entries.explanation: This passage highlights the importance of putting your full effort into your tasks today. Life is temporary, and the chance to work, plan, or learn doesn’t continue indefinitely. On an ordinary Tuesday, this might mean focusing wholeheartedly on a project at your job or tackling household chores with enthusiasm. The idea is to engage fully in what you’re doing now, recognizing that your opportunity to contribute and create is a gift of the present moment.
entries.question: What task can you focus on fully today?

entries.verseWEB: Let the favor of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands.
entries.verseKJV: And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
entries.pullShort: Establish the work of our hands.
entries.pullMedium: Let the favor of the Lord our God be on us.
entries.pullLong: Let the favor of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands for us.
entries.explanation: Moses has just spent a whole psalm on how short life is, grass in the morning, gone by evening. Then he ends with this ask: establish the work of our hands. Make something we did outlast us. Anyone who has finished a long day and wondered whether any of it mattered has prayed some version of it. You do the work that is yours. The lasting part, the psalm admits, was always going to be a gift.
entries.question: How do you seek meaning in your daily tasks?

entries.verseWEB: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.
entries.verseKJV: And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.
entries.pullShort: work heartily, as for the Lord
entries.pullMedium: work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men
entries.pullLong: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward
entries.explanation: Paul addresses those who may feel their work is unnoticed or undervalued. He reframes the perspective: the true audience of your efforts isn't merely your employer or colleagues, but a higher purpose. On a regular Tuesday, this might mean finding meaning in routine tasks, knowing that your diligence and integrity matter beyond immediate recognition. It's not about receiving earthly applause but understanding the deeper significance of your contributions.
entries.question: Where do you find meaning in daily tasks?

entries.verseWEB: “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
entries.verseKJV: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
entries.pullShort: Well done, good and faithful servant.
entries.pullMedium: You have been faithful over a few things.
entries.pullLong: Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things.
entries.explanation: This line lands in the middle of a story: a servant trusted with a little, faithful with it, welcomed with the words well done. Notice what gets praised. Not scale, faithfulness. The unglamorous jobs done properly when nobody was checking. Most of your life is made of exactly that, the small commitment kept, the errand done fully. The story says those are not the boring part before the real assignment. They are the assignment.
entries.question: Where can you be more consistent today?

entries.verseWEB: Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest.
entries.verseKJV: Therefore said he unto them, The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest.
entries.pullMedium: The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few.
entries.pullLong: The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest...
entries.explanation: Jesus speaks to his followers about a challenge and an opportunity. The work to be done is vast, and the number of people ready to do it is small. Think of a busy day at work or a project deadline when everyone is stretched thin. Jesus isn't telling you to do it all alone. Instead, he suggests asking for help from a higher power, acknowledging that the task is bigger than any one person.
entries.question: Who can you ask for help today?

entries.verseWEB: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
entries.verseKJV: And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
entries.pullShort: Don't be weary in doing good.
entries.pullMedium: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap.
entries.pullLong: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
entries.explanation: When you're doing good but feeling exhausted, it can seem like your efforts don't matter. This passage offers encouragement to continue, even when the results aren't visible yet. On a typical Tuesday, this might mean continuing to help a colleague or volunteer your time, even if you don't see immediate change. The reassurance is that persistence in good actions will eventually lead to a positive outcome. It's a reminder that small acts of kindness do add up.
entries.question: Where do you feel like giving up today?

entries.verseWEB: Honor the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase; so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.
entries.verseKJV: Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.
entries.pullShort: Honor the LORD with your substance
entries.pullMedium: Honor the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits
entries.pullLong: Honor the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase; so your barns will be filled
entries.explanation: This proverb speaks to the idea of prioritizing what you value. When you budget your paycheck, consider what you place first. For the ancient audience, the 'first fruits' were the best of their harvest, a priority, not leftovers. On a regular Tuesday, maybe it’s about setting aside a bit of your paycheck to help someone or support a cause you care about. The principle here is prioritizing what really matters to you.
entries.question: What do you prioritize with your income?

entries.verseWEB: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
entries.verseKJV: There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
entries.pullShort: He who waters shall be watered...
entries.pullMedium: The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters...
entries.pullLong: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
entries.explanation: This proverb watches two kinds of people: the open handed, whose lives keep growing wider, and the tight fisted, whose lives shrink around what they guard. It is an observation about what giving does to the giver, not a bargain with returns. Sharing your lunch with a coworker who forgot theirs costs you half a sandwich and leaves you more open than it found you. A closed hand protects, but it also cannot receive.
entries.question: Where could you be more generous today?

entries.verseWEB: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
entries.verseKJV: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
entries.pullMedium: Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven...
entries.pullLong: Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal.
entries.explanation: This passage addresses people who often lost possessions to decay or theft, a real concern. It highlights a choice about what's truly valuable. Earthly treasures are vulnerable, impermanent. Instead, investing in intangible, enduring values—kindness, generosity—builds a legacy beyond physical reach. Perhaps on a Tuesday, as you consider a purchase or a donation, reflect on what holds lasting significance. It's about where your heart finds its true home.
entries.question: What do you consider your true treasure?

entries.verseWEB: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.
entries.verseKJV: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
entries.pullShort: No one can serve two masters
entries.pullMedium: You can’t serve both God and Mammon.
entries.pullLong: No one can serve two masters... You can’t serve both God and Mammon.
entries.explanation: In this passage, Jesus addresses the challenge of divided loyalties. Serving two masters means your attention and energy are split, leading to frustration and imbalance. Picture a typical day where your work demands clash with family time. Prioritizing one might come at the expense of the other. Jesus highlights that pursuing wealth can distract you from deeper values and connections. The takeaway here is about focus and where your true commitments lie.
entries.question: What divides your attention and loyalty today?

entries.verseWEB: He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
entries.verseKJV: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
